title: Particles and Interjections
description: Use interrogatives, conjunctions, negation, and interjections.

blocks.caption: Summary
blocks.html: The particles are mostly worn-down nouns — either whole or disintegrated — though some are proper interjections or demonstratives. Because they are nouns they stand, when in relation, in the construct state, with the word they govern in the genitive. From this single idea flow the many uses of Hebrew's small words: the inseparable prefixes, the interrogative הֲ, the suffixes, the adverbs, the conjunctions, the negatives, the oath-formulas, and the interjections.

blocks.caption: The nature of particles
blocks.html:
Particles are mostly nouns, whole or worn down. Being nouns, they stand in the construct state when they govern a following word, which is then in the genitive — though Hebrew does not mark case endings, so this is more a way of thinking about them than a visible form. Some particles are so feeble that they cannot stand alone but prefix themselves to a noun or pronoun; others are inseparable affixes.

This description is a useful way to understand why many particles form tight units with what follows. Some survive as independent words; others are fragments that can no longer stand alone. Several take the same kinds of pronominal suffixes found on nouns and prepositions. The suffix expresses the participant related to that particle, while the particle supplies the relation. Learn the whole attached form in context rather than trying to translate each letter separately.

blocks.caption: The interrogative prefix
blocks.html:
The interrogative הֲ is an inseparable prefix that turns a statement into a question: הֲזֶה (is this?). Its pointing varies — usually הֲ, but before a simple shewa it is הֶ, and before gutturals the vowel adjusts. This single prefixed letter is the ordinary sign of a direct or indirect question.

Because the interrogative is attached, it can be easy to overlook at the beginning of a long pointed word. Check for it before parsing the noun or verb that follows. Its vowel is not perfectly uniform: the following consonant's shewa or guttural affects the pointing, so a changed vowel does not necessarily indicate a different interrogative particle. The syntax and context tell you whether the clause is a question rather than a statement.

blocks.caption: Conjunctions and negation
blocks.html:
The common conjunctions are אוֹ (or) and אִם (if); "whether … or" is אִם … אוֹ or a doubled form. "But" is very often expressed by simple waw; a stronger "but" is אוּלָם. After a negative, "but" is אִם כִּי. Negation of a command or wish uses אַל, distinct from לֹא (not), which negates an ordinary statement.

Conjunctions often work in pairs. Watch for the first member of a construction such as “either … or,” “both … and,” or “neither … nor,” then look for its partner; translating only the first word can leave the relationship unclear. Waw is usually “and,” but Davidson notes that it can carry a contrast equivalent to “but.” The stronger particle אוּלָם makes that contrast explicit. After a negative, אִם כִּי can also introduce “but,” so a particle's function must be read from the construction, not its dictionary gloss alone.

blocks.caption: Adverbs and interjections
blocks.html:
Many adverbs are directly connected with nouns and end in -ām, an old accusative ending: יוֹמָם (by day), חִנָּם (in vain). Others are the noun סָבִיב (circuit), used as "round about". The interjections are few but vivid: הוֹי and אוֹי (ah!, alas!), הִנֵּה (behold), and הֶאָח (ha!). In oaths, אִם means "certainly not" and אִם־לֹא "certainly".

The same surface form can belong to different grammatical uses. An adverb may have grown from a noun, a preposition may be extended into a conjunction, and an interjection may stand alone as an emotional response. Identify what the word connects to: a noun phrase, a clause, a question, or no syntactic partner. In an oath, אִם / אִם־לֹא is idiomatic and does not have its ordinary “if / if not” force; Davidson explains it as an abbreviated conditional oath. Translate the whole formula, not its pieces word for word.

blocks.caption: Common confusion
blocks.html: Do not force a single English word onto each particle. The same small word serves as conjunction, adverb, or interjection according to its place. Read the particle in its construction — the interrogative turns a clause into a question, waw may mean "but", and אִם shifts from "if" to an oath-formula — and let the context choose.
